q: A cluster of nineteenth-century bodegas still stands around one railway station in Rioja Alta. Which town?
exp: The Barrio de la Estacion grew up around the rail link that carried wine to France, and several of Rioja's oldest houses sit within a few hundred metres of each other.

q: Which of these is the minimum time a red Rioja Crianza must spend in cask?
exp: Twelve months in oak within twenty-four months of total ageing. Spain's national floor for Crianza is only six months in wood, so a Rioja Crianza is a stricter wine than the word promises elsewhere.

q: Five years of ageing, at least two in cask and three more in bottle, earn a red Rioja which designation?
exp: Most houses declare it only in vintages they believe will repay the wait. The long spell in bottle is why a Gran Reserva often reaches the table already mature.

q: What limits the size of the casks that may count toward Spain's ageing terms?
opts: Nothing, only the species of wood is fixed
exp: A large cask gives far less oxygen and extract per litre of wine, so ageing in one would not deliver what the term promises. The 225-litre barrica remains the working standard.

q: A sommelier says Spain's ageing terms are unusual in European wine law. What makes them so?
opts: They name the grape varieties the wine may contain
They may be used only in Rioja and Ribera del Duero
Cask and bottle minimums are set nationally in law
A tasting panel awards each wine a quality score
exp: Elsewhere the term is defined appellation by appellation, if at all. Spain fixes one set of cask and bottle minimums nationally, which many denominations then tighten and the Consejo checks, so the words compare across bodegas.

q: Ordering Rioja's red ageing classes by the total time each demands, which sequence is correct?
exp: Nothing required, then two years, then three, then five. The ladder measures elapsed time and nothing else, so a superb young wine from a great site still sits at the bottom of it.

q: Beyond its time in cask, a red Rioja Reserva must also rest in bottle before release. What is that minimum?
exp: Three years in total, of which at least twelve months in cask and at least six in bottle. The bottle rule is what stops a wine going straight from barrel to shelf.

q: Frost can strike in late May and again in September on the high plateau around Aranda de Duero. Which denomination farms it?
exp: Vineyards run from roughly 750 to 900 metres, so nights stay cold and the season is short. That gap between day heat and night cold is what holds colour and acidity in Tinto Fino.

q: Downstream from Ribera del Duero the valley turns hotter and drier and the reds grow heavier. Which denomination sits there?
exp: Toro lies in Zamora province, where Tempranillo is called Tinta de Toro and gives dense, high-alcohol wine. Sandy soils there let some ungrafted old vines survive phylloxera.

q: One Castilian estate was making a Bordeaux-influenced red for over a century before any denomination existed around it. Which estate?
exp: Founded in the 1860s and famous for Unico, it blends Tinto Fino with Cabernet Sauvignon and other Bordeaux varieties. Ribera del Duero itself was granted DO status only in 1982.

q: The river behind these Castilian denominations changes its name at the Portuguese border. What does it become?
exp: Duero and Douro are one river. It runs west past Ribera del Duero, Rueda and Toro before cutting the schist gorges where Port is grown.

q: A Ribera del Duero red is usually darker and firmer in tannin than a Rioja of the same age. Which factor explains most of that?
opts: A large share of Garnacha in the blend
The altitude, and the wide swing from day heat to night cold
A longer minimum cask ageing set by the denomination
exp: Cold nights near 800 metres slow the loss of acid and thicken the skins, so the fruit arrives with more colour and tannin. Rioja's lower, more Atlantic sites give a lighter frame.

q: Vines dig through crumbling black slate on terraces around a ruined Carthusian priory. Which denomination is this?
exp: The soil is called llicorella and the priory is Scala Dei, which gave the region its name. Yields are tiny and the wines come out dense, high in alcohol and stony.

q: Which denomination forms a horseshoe around Priorat and is often sold as its affordable neighbour?
exp: Montsant was carved out of the old Tarragona denomination and shares varieties and much of the climate, though only part of it sits on the same slate.

q: Trepat is grown almost nowhere else and goes into pink wine. Which Catalan denomination is its home?
exp: Conca de Barbera is Trepat's stronghold. The variety is permitted for rosado Cava but not for white, and it gives pale colour, low tannin and bright red-fruit aromatics.

q: Which Catalan denomination climbs from the Mediterranean shore to eight hundred metres inland, so that one estate can grow Xarel-lo low down and Parellada high up?
exp: Penedes divides into a coastal, a central and a high zone. That spread of altitude is much of why Sant Sadurni d'Anoia grew into the heart of the sparkling trade, and it makes serious still wine besides.
